name: ADRs / design docs
description:
Write down the why, not just the what — future me is the main audience. Lightweight ADRs beat tribal memory, and a regular design-review cadence is what turns them from a graveyard into a decision log: bring the interfaces and the trade-offs, not the finished code.

Adopt as a habit, not a tool. The cost is a page per real decision and a review people actually attend; skip it for reversible, local changes and spend the time on the one-way doors.

name: API contracts & lifecycle
description:
Design the interface first and treat it as a product: explicit contracts (OpenAPI, Protobuf), consumer-driven contract tests, a real versioning policy, and an actual deprecation and sunset process. Adding is safe; changing and removing is where callers break.

Adopt for anything with more than one consumer or a life longer than one team's attention span. The cost is the discipline of not breaking callers, which is far cheaper than coordinated releases.

name: Continuous delivery
description:
Small, always-releasable changes through an automated pipeline. Deploys should be boring, frequent and reversible.

Automating versioning and changelogs from commit messages (semantic-release and similar) is a nice-to-have once commit discipline exists — not a substitute for it.

name: Cost engineering
description:
Cost is a design constraint, not a monthly surprise: know the unit economics of a request or a tenant, tag resources for allocation, set budget alarms, and prefer architectures whose cost tracks usage. Cheapest at design time, most expensive as an incident.

Adopt for anything that will run long enough to bill; skip only for genuinely fixed-cost experiments.

name: Feature flags
description: Decouple deploy from release and make rollback a config change. Adopt for anything risky or user-facing.

name: Infrastructure as Code
description: Non-negotiable for anything beyond a scratch environment: reviewed, versioned, reproducible infrastructure. Manual console changes are how you get drift and outages.

name: Monorepo
description:
Default for related projects: atomic changes, shared tooling, one CI.

Adopt when the projects genuinely change together; split when they don't. A caching task runner (Turborepo and friends) earns its place once the graph is big enough to page in — below that, plain scripts and CI caching do the job.

name: Observability
description: Emit structured events, traces and metrics from day one. Debugging anything on-call without them is guesswork.

name: Pair programming
description: The best tool I know for spreading knowledge and catching mistakes early. Adopt for tricky or high-risk work — not all day, every day.

name: Reliability: SLOs & error budgets
description:
Pick the few journeys that matter, set service-level objectives, and treat the error budget as the release gate: when it is spent, reliability work beats new features. Tie it to on-call, incident response and blameless postmortems, and rehearse restores against explicit RTO and RPO targets instead of assuming backups work.

The cost is measurement and discipline. Adopt once anything is user-facing; skip only for genuinely throwaway systems.

name: Reproducible environments
description:
The same environment from laptop to CI to production, declared in-repo: Docker Compose for the local multi-service stack, dev containers or cloud workspaces for per-task isolation, and Nix where the system itself has to be pinned. It is the real answer to "works on my machine", and the prerequisite for letting new joiners or agents run checks anywhere.

Cost is maintaining the environment definition; worth it as soon as more than one person or machine runs the code. Stop where a serverless deploy or a single compiled binary genuinely needs no environment.

name: Resilience patterns
description:
Assume every remote call fails: timeouts on everything, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency keys so retries are safe, circuit breakers and bulkheads so one dependency cannot take down the rest, and load shedding or backpressure instead of unbounded queues. Design the degradation path, not just the happy one.

No real cost beyond discipline; the failure mode of skipping it is an outage. Revisit thresholds as traffic and the dependency count grow.

name: Security engineering
description:
Shift security left as engineering rather than a gate: threat modelling on new designs, least privilege with short-lived credentials and OIDC instead of long-lived keys, secrets in a manager rather than env files, and a supply chain you can attest to — dependency review, SBOM, signed artifacts.

Adopt everywhere. The cost is ongoing hygiene; the cost of skipping it is discovered on the worst possible day.

name: Service boundaries
description:
Start with a modular monolith and split only when a boundary has earned it: separate scaling, ownership, release cadence or failure isolation. Microservices are a packaging decision, not an architecture; splitting too early buys a distributed monolith and the operational bill to match. Move incrementally — strangler fig rather than rewrite.

Revisit boundaries as the team topology changes; Conway's law is not optional.

name: Testing strategy
description:
Decide the shape deliberately: many fast unit and component tests, a thin end-to-end layer, and contract tests at service boundaries so two services can agree without a full environment. Flaky tests are a defect in the pipeline, not a nuisance to retry.

Adopt as a position. The runners and frameworks matter far less than where each kind of test sits, what it is allowed to touch, and who owns it when it breaks.

name: Docker
description:
Default way to package and run anything, dev and prod. The image is the unit of deployment, and Compose is the default way to run that image plus its dependencies locally — if a stack cannot run under Compose, that is usually a smell worth fixing.

Avoid only where a serverless deploy or a single compiled binary is genuinely simpler.

name: OpenTelemetry
description: Default instrumentation format for traces, metrics and logs — vendor-neutral, so I'm not locked to one backend. Instrument once, ship wherever.

name: Terraform
description:
Default for provisioning cloud infrastructure: declarative, reviewable and state-tracked. OpenTofu is the hedge if licensing becomes a problem.

I'd avoid it for dynamic, high-churn resources better managed from the application or from Kubernetes manifests.

name: AWS
description:
Default cloud. I know it, it has everything, and the boring services — S3, RDS, SQS, Lambda — are reliable. GCP is capable, but it is not where my operational familiarity or the ecosystem momentum sits, so I would only go there for a specific product. Keep the application portable enough that provider choice stays reversible.

Cost and complexity are the price.

name: GitHub
description: Default home for code, review, issues and CI. Network effects make it the obvious choice.

name: Linux
description: Everything I deploy runs here, and with containers and Nix it's a workable dev target too.

name: Node.js
description:
Default runtime for TypeScript/JavaScript work, server and CLI alike. One language across the stack is the main draw.

I'd move to Go when I need predictable throughput or a small container image.

name: React
description:
Still my default view layer: the component model, ecosystem and my familiarity make me productive immediately.

I'd avoid it for essentially static pages where plain HTML or a server-rendered template carries far less machinery.

name: Tauri
description:
Default for desktop apps: a React front end over a Rust core, with small binaries and no bundled browser.

Used it for a run of launchers and it's my go-to over Electron.

name: TypeScript
description:
Default for anything with a UI or a browser in the loop. Types catch the class of bug I actually hit, and the tooling is the best in class.

Not worth the ceremony for throwaway scripts.

name: Agentic delivery
description:
Agents as a real part of the delivery loop: tools, context and multi-step goals rather than fancy autocomplete, and a pipeline where a well-specified change goes in and a reviewed change comes out, gated by strong automated checks. Humans keep the design, the interfaces and the final call.

Trial: promising on well-specified, well-tested, low-ambiguity work; not for requirements still being discovered or failures that are expensive. The checks are what make it safe, so invest there first.

name: AI in production
description:
Shipping AI as a dependency, not just using it to write code: evaluations as tests, guardrails against prompt injection and unsafe output, and a deliberate choice between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning. Route and fall back across models, watch cost and latency per request, and treat context and retrieval like any other data pipeline — including privacy and leakage.

Trial: the capability is real, the operating practices are still forming. Keep a human on the failure path for anything consequential.

name: Data architecture & schema evolution
description:
Treat data as a product with an owner, a schema and a lifecycle: versioned migrations, backward-compatible schema evolution, data contracts between producers and consumers, and explicit retention, privacy and residency rules. Separate transactional from analytical workloads before reporting queries start hurting production.

Trial while the practices settle per stack; the cost of skipping it compounds every time a schema changes under a live consumer.

name: Delivery metrics
description:
Measure the pipeline, not the people: lead time for change, deployment frequency, change failure rate and time to restore, plus the developer-experience signals that explain them. Numbers make "we need to slow down" arguable with evidence rather than opinion.

Trial: cheap to start and genuinely useful, but easy to weaponise. Keep it about the system, agree the definitions, and do not trust a trend before you trust the data.

name: Event-driven architecture
description:
Async, event-based flows where the coupling and latency profile justify them: an outbox instead of dual writes, sagas for multi-step transactions, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues and deliberate ordering. Exactly-once delivery is a myth; at-least-once plus idempotency is the real target.

Trial: powerful and easy to get subtly wrong. Adopt per bounded context once you can observe and replay the stream, not as a default for the whole system.

name: Progressive delivery
description:
Decouple release from deploy further than feature flags: canary and blue/green rollouts, automated rollback, and fault injection so a bad change is contained to a fraction of traffic. Continuous delivery gets the change out; progressive delivery decides how much blast radius it gets.

Trial: the mechanics are well understood, but doing them well needs good telemetry and automation, and testing in production only works when you can observe and reverse quickly.

name: Coding agents
description:
One position for the agent CLI in my terminal: Pi is the default, with Claude Code, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot as alternatives depending on provider and limits. What matters is the shape — a small, hackable agent that runs the model against real tools (read, edit, bash) with the session and the diff in front of me — not which vendor ships it.

Trial: useful enough to reach for on anything where I keep the design and review the output, and still young enough that I do not hand it the controls. This is the fastest-aging cluster on the radar; expect the names to rotate, so hold the position, not the brand.

name: Cloudflare
description:
DNS, Workers, R2 and the rest are fast, cheap and pleasant to use.

Trial because I don't want to depend on a single edge provider for core infrastructure.

name: Kubernetes
description:
Valuable once there are many services and a platform team, but it's a lot of machinery for a small system.

Trial: happy to use it on real work with managed control planes, and I'd avoid running it by hand for one or two services.

name: Model gateway
description:
A gateway in front of models — OpenRouter and similar — giving one API across frontier and open models, with cheap and free options that make agentic work affordable to run all day, plus routing and fallbacks. It keeps model choice a config decision instead of a rewrite.

Trial: ideal for experiments and choosing a model per task, but keep a direct provider path for anything important so the gateway stays a convenience rather than a single point of failure.

name: Expo
description:
How I build mobile and TV apps — Expo's tooling makes the setup and build story painless.

Trial because the ecosystem churn and native escape hatches still cost real time on anything non-trivial.

name: Go
description:
Where I'd go for small, fast services and CLI tools: quick builds, a single static binary, straightforward concurrency.

Still a trial rather than a default because the type system and dependency ergonomics are a step down from what I'd like.

name: Next.js
description:
Used it across several web apps; file-based routing and SSR are genuinely handy when I need them.

Trial — for most of what I build, a plain React SPA on Vite is lighter.

name: Accessibility & i18n
description:
Accessibility and internationalisation as architectural constraints, not a later pass: semantic structure and keyboard paths, text externalised from the start, locale-aware dates, currency and layout, and tests that cover both. Retrofitting either is a rewrite of the view layer.

Assess where the audience or the regulation demands it; the cost is discipline up front, and the cost of delay is much larger.

name: Platform engineering
description:
An internal developer platform treated as a product: golden paths and paved roads that make the right thing the easy thing, clear ownership boundaries, and self-service for the common cases. The alternative is every team re-solving deployment, observability and CI on its own.

Assess: real leverage once there are several teams, but a platform team that ships mandates instead of paths is worse than none.

name: Trunk-based development
description:
Short-lived branches and frequent merges are where I want to be, but it leans on strong CI and feature flags.

Assessing how far I can push it without breaking flow.

name: Managed app platforms
description:
Managed app hosting — Vercel, Netlify, Railway and similar — for prototypes, side projects and small frontends where the developer experience is excellent and shipping fast is the point. The architectural question is not which vendor ranks best but exit cost: pricing cliffs, egress, and how much of the app is portable to another host.

Assess for anything with real traffic or a long life; adopt only when lock-in is acceptable because the app is small or genuinely disposable.

name: C
description: Retro and homelab tinkering territory. I enjoy it for low-level experiments, but it's not something I want to maintain in production.

name: Kotlin
description: Where I'd go for Android work and native mobile features. One active project so far; still learning the idiom.

name: Rust
description:
Interesting for performance-critical or memory-sensitive pieces, but I haven't shipped anything meaningful in it.

Watching, not committing — the learning cost is real.

name: Microservices first
description:
Splitting into services before the boundaries are known. You pay the distributed-systems tax — network failures, partial failure, versioning, observability, deployment coordination — before you get any of the benefits, and you usually get a distributed monolith. Prefer a modular monolith until a boundary earns its own deployment.

Revisit per context when separate scaling, ownership or failure isolation is a measured need rather than an aspiration.

name: Shared database across services
description:
A database read and written directly by several services. It couples their schemas and releases, makes independent deploys a fiction, and turns every migration into a cross-team negotiation. Integrate through an interface or a published event stream instead.

Revisit only as a deliberate, temporary migration step — never as the steady state.

name: TDD
description:
I want the safety net, but writing tests first isn't how I actually work and pretending otherwise wastes time. Prefer test-after plus strong types and integration tests.

Revisit for gnarly logic where the design pressure genuinely helps.
